claims.text: Superior high-temperature oxidation resistance in high-entropy alloys is driven by preferential surface segregation of high oxygen-affinity elements such as Cr or Al.
Surface-segregated Cr or Al promotes formation of a continuous, slow-growing protective oxide scale.
The initial high-entropy alloy has a homogeneous distribution of multiple alloying elements, including elements with high oxygen affinity.
The alloy is to be exposed to a high-temperature, oxygen-rich environment.
Testing should be conducted above approximately 700°C at fixed oxygen partial pressure.
A conventional alloy with similar elemental makeup but lower compositional complexity should be used as the control.
High-temperature exposure causes high oxygen-affinity elements to segregate to the surface and form a protective oxide phase.
Elevated temperature facilitates migration of high oxygen-affinity elements toward the alloy surface.
Surface enrichment in high oxygen-affinity elements drives nucleation and growth of a continuous oxide layer.
The continuous oxide layer acts as a diffusion barrier and thereby slows further oxidation.
The high-entropy alloy will form a dense, continuous protective oxide layer that grows slowly with time.
Under identical conditions, baseline alloys will form oxide scales that are less continuous or grow more rapidly than those on the high-entropy alloy.
The proposed baseline alloys lack significant elemental-segregation mechanisms.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate under oxidative conditions above approximately 700°C.
Applicability of the mechanism at lower temperatures or in non-oxidative environments is uncertain.
The quantitative contribution of segregation kinetics and the effects of individual alloying elements are uncertain.
Surface composition profiles, oxide continuity and thickness, and time-dependent oxide growth kinetics can test the proposed segregation-mediated mechanism.
Failure to observe both significant surface segregation and a more continuous, slower-growing oxide than the control would falsify the hypothesis.
